etymology: From Middle English snoffe, the charred end of a burning wick; rendering Hebrew malqāchayim and mezammērōth, the golden shears made to crop the spent wick of the sanctuary lamps.
biblical_def: Snuffers are the small golden shears wrought for the candlestick of the tabernacle and temple, made to crop the charred wick so the flame should burn clean and bright. They stand in the inventory of pure gold: “And he made his seven lamps, and his snuffers, and his snuffdishes, of pure gold” (Exo 37:23), and again among Solomon’s holy vessels, “the snuffers, and the basons, and the spoons, and the censers of pure gold” (1Ki 7:50). So slight a tool that in the days of Joash the repair-money made no snuffers of it (2Ki 12:13), yet the sanctuary could not do without them; for the light that was to burn continually before the LORD would smoke and dim if the burnt wick were never trimmed. Herein lies the lesson of the snuffers: the lamp of testimony is not left to itself but tended, and the hand that tends it is the LORD’s. Christ walks in the midst of the golden candlesticks and trims His churches (Rev 1—3), cropping what is charred and dead that the flame may shine the clearer. What the flesh calls loss—the pruning, the paring away—is the snuffing of the wick, that His people burn without smoke. He will not quench the smoking flax (Isa 42:3); He trims it. The instrument was of pure gold, for even the meanest office about the light of God is holy.
webster_summary: The golden shears of the sanctuary, made to crop the burnt wick so the lamp should burn clean and bright.
webster_full: SNUFFERS, an instrument for cropping the snuff, or charred end of the wick, of a lamp or candle.
In Scripture, part of the pure-gold furniture of the candlestick (Exo 37:23; 1Ki 7:50).
Reckoned among the holy vessels not renewed from the temple repair-money (2Ki 12:13).
Their office was to keep the continual light clear of smoke, not to quench it.
A figure of the LORD’s tending of His lamps, cropping the dead that the flame may shine.

corruption_summary: A tool of the candlestick, not a contested doctrine; the snuffers recover the truth that the light of God is tended, and tended by pruning.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the snuffers rebuke is the modern love of a flame that never needs cropping—a religion of feeling that resents every paring, calling the LORD’s discipline cruelty and the pruning-knife an enemy. But the wick that is never trimmed does not burn brighter; it smokes, gutters, and goes out. The age would keep the charred wick and blame the smoke on God; the sanctuary teaches that the light burns clean only where the dead is cropped away.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the light of testimony is kept, not spontaneous: the LORD gave golden shears with the golden lamps, and He who lit the flame also tends it. Every affliction that crops the flesh is a snuffer in His hand, that His people, and His churches, may shine the brighter before Him (Heb 12:11).

usage: The light that is to burn continually is not left to itself, but trimmed.
What the flesh calls loss is often the snuffing of the wick, that we burn without smoke.
Even the meanest office about the light of God is wrought of pure gold.

etymology: A compound of flesh and hook, rendering Hebrew mazlēg—the three-tined forks of brass (and, in the temple, of gold) used to handle the flesh of the sacrifices upon the altar.
biblical_def: Fleshhooks are the pronged forks of the altar, appointed among its brazen vessels: “And thou shalt make his pans to receive his ashes, and his shovels, and his basons, and his fleshhooks, and his firepans: all the vessels thereof thou shalt make of brass” (Exo 27:3). When the camp moved they were borne with the rest of the altar’s furniture (Num 4:14), and in the temple David appointed pure gold for them (1Ch 28:17). Their use was to lift and turn the flesh of the offerings as it seethed, that the portions might be rightly handled and rightly divided. Yet the same instrument bears a warning, for at Shiloh the sons of Eli made the fleshhook an engine of greed: “the priest’s servant came, while the flesh was in seething, with a fleshhook of three teeth in his hand” (1Sa 2:13), and thrust it in to seize for themselves what belonged to the LORD. So a holy tool became the mark of an unholy priesthood, and the LORD swore judgment on the house of Eli. The fleshhook thus preaches on both edges: that God ordains order and means about His altar, and that the vessels of the sanctuary are no license for the servant to serve himself. What is given to handle the holy things must handle them in fear, lest the ministry be turned to gain.
webster_summary: The three-tined altar-forks of brass or gold, used to handle the flesh of the sacrifices—and, at Shiloh, turned to greed.
webster_full: FLESHHOOKS, forks or hooks, commonly of three tines, for taking up flesh from a vessel or altar.
Numbered among the brazen vessels of the altar (Exo 27:3; Exo 38:3).
Borne with the altar’s furniture when the camp journeyed (Num 4:14).
Made of pure gold in David’s pattern for the temple (1Ch 28:17).
At Shiloh made an instrument of priestly greed against the LORD (1Sa 2:13-17).

corruption_summary: A brazen tool of the altar, not a contested doctrine; yet the fleshhook recovers a solemn warning against turning holy office to private gain.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse the fleshhook rebukes is the ancient sin of Hophni and Phinehas—making the ministry a trade and the altar a table for the self. Where men handle sacred things for what they can draw off, the fleshhook of three teeth is thrust into the LORD’s portion; the age is full of such hooks, dressed as service, that seethe with covetousness. The vessel is holy; the hand that grasps for itself is not.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is reverence in office: God ordains order, tools, and means about His worship, and those who minister at the altar must handle the holy things in fear, not in greed (1Sa 2:17). The fleshhook was to serve the offering, never to rob it.
roots_summary: The three-tined altar-forks, Hebrew mazlēg, of brass and of gold, made to handle the flesh of the sacrifices.
roots_lines: Fleshhooks — flesh + hook; Hebrew mazlēg, a forked implement.

usage: God ordains order and means about His altar; the fleshhook was for handling, not hoarding.

etymology: A compound of fire and pan, rendering Hebrew machtāh—a pan or shovel for carrying live coals; the same word is elsewhere rendered censer and snuffdish, the vessel taking its name from its use.
biblical_def: Firepans are the brazen coal-vessels of the altar, made to carry the burning coals whereby the fire of God was kept and served: “his fleshhooks, and his firepans: all the vessels thereof thou shalt make of brass” (Exo 27:3), and so Bezaleel wrought them (Exo 38:3). When the camp journeyed they were reckoned among “all the vessels of the altar” and covered for the march (Num 4:14). The Hebrew word behind firepan is the same that is elsewhere Englished censer and snuffdish; the vessel is named from what it holds—fire. Herein is the altar’s great theme: the fire upon it was not kindled by man but came down from the LORD (Lev 9:24), and it was to be kept burning and never to go out (Lev 6:13). The firepan is the servant of that fire, bearing the sacred coals to and fro that the flame be neither lost nor scattered. When Babylon at last plundered the house of God, “the firepans, and the bowls… the captain of the guard took away” (2Ki 25:15)—the very vessels of the holy fire carried off to a strange land. So the firepan preaches the guarding of the fire of worship: kindled from heaven, kept by appointed means, and grievously lost when a people forsake the LORD who lit it.
webster_summary: The brazen coal-vessels of the altar, made to carry the sacred fire that came down from heaven and was never to go out.
webster_full: FIREPANS, pans or shovels for carrying live coals of fire.
Numbered among the brazen vessels of the altar (Exo 27:3; Exo 38:3).
The Hebrew word is elsewhere rendered censer and snuffdish, named from its use.

Carried off among the spoils when Babylon took the temple (2Ki 25:15).

corruption_summary: A vessel of the altar-fire, not a contested doctrine; the firepan recovers the truth that the fire of worship is kindled from heaven and kept by appointed means.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the firepan rebukes is the age’s appetite for strange fire—worship kindled from the self, warmed by novelty and feeling, owing nothing to the LORD who alone sends down the flame. Men would carry their own coals into the sanctuary and call the smoke devotion. But the fire on God’s altar was His gift, His command, and His to keep; a firepan bearing common fire is no nearer to Him for all its brass.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the guarding of the holy fire: it came down from heaven (Lev 9:24), it was never to go out (Lev 6:13), and it was borne only in the vessels God appointed. Worship is kept, not improvised; and a people that forsakes the LORD may find its very firepans carried into captivity (2Ki 25:15).
roots_summary: Brazen coal-vessels of the altar, Hebrew machtāh, made to carry the sacred fire that never went out.

etymology: From Old French censier, from Latin incensum, that which is burned; rendering Hebrew machtāh and miqtēreth—the fire-pan in which coals were bare that incense might be burned before the LORD.
biblical_def: A censer is the vessel for burning incense, a pan of brass or gold in which live coals were carried that the sweet perfume might rise before the LORD. Of all the vessels of the sanctuary the censer is the most solemnly bound up with judgment, for by it men drew near to God, and by it presumptuous men perished. Nadab and Abihu “took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not” (Lev 10:1), and fire came out and devoured them. Korah and his company were bidden take every man his censer (Num 16:17), and the earth swallowed them, their two hundred and fifty censers being beaten into plates for the altar as a sign. King Uzziah, no priest, took a censer to burn incense and the leprosy rose in his forehead (2Ch 26:19). Yet the censer is also the vessel of acceptance: in heaven an angel stands at the altar “having a golden censer… that he should offer it with the prayers of all saints” (Rev 8:3), for incense is the figure of prayer (Psa 141:2). The censer therefore divides the near: incense the LORD appoints ascends as a sweet savour; incense of man’s own devising is strange fire, and it consumes. The nearer the worship, the deadlier the presumption.
webster_summary: The vessel of incense—by which the appointed draw near with a sweet savour, and by which the presumptuous offer strange fire and perish.
webster_full: CENSERS, vessels or pans in which incense is burned upon live coals.
Of brass or of pure gold among the vessels of the sanctuary (1Ki 7:50).
The instrument of Nadab and Abihu’s strange fire (Lev 10:1) and of Korah’s revolt (Num 16:17).
By a censer unlawfully taken, Uzziah was smitten with leprosy (2Ch 26:19).
In heaven the golden censer offers the incense of the prayers of the saints (Rev 8:3).

corruption_summary: The censer carries a genuine and living corruption: will-worship—the strange fire of worship men invent, offered before the LORD which He commanded not.
corruption_paragraphs: The strange fire of Nadab and Abihu is not a dead antiquity but a present sin. Wherever men worship God after a fashion He never commanded—offering the censer of their own invention, their own fire, their own will—they repeat the offence, however sincere the smoke. The age loves worship that pleases the worshipper, that answers to feeling and fashion rather than to the word; it calls this freedom. Scripture calls it will-worship (Col 2:23), and names the fire strange. That the LORD “commanded them not” was the whole of their guilt, for in His worship what He has not commanded He has forbidden.

The censer also rebukes the seizing of an office not given. Korah grasped a priesthood he was not called to; Uzziah, a king, seized a censer that belonged to the sons of Aaron, and went out a leper. Against every self-appointed nearness the vessel testifies that God chooses His own priests and appoints His own worship. The remedy is the true and golden Censer, the great High Priest through whose merit alone our incense rises accepted (Rev 8:3; Heb 10:19-22); apart from His appointment, the nearer men press the more surely the fire devours.
roots_summary: Fire-pans of incense, Hebrew machtāh, that both carry the sweet savour of appointed prayer and the strange fire of presumption.

usage: Incense the LORD appoints ascends a sweet savour; incense of man’s devising is strange fire.
In the worship of God, what He has not commanded He has forbidden.
The nearer the worship, the deadlier the presumption; only in Christ does our incense rise accepted.

etymology: From Old English scofl, an implement for lifting and casting; rendering Hebrew yā'—the brazen scoops of the altar, made to lift away the fat ashes of the burnt offerings.
biblical_def: Shovels are the brazen scoops of the altar, appointed to lift and carry away the ashes of the sacrifices: “his pans to receive his ashes, and his shovels, and his basons… all the vessels thereof thou shalt make of brass” (Exo 27:3), and so they were wrought (Exo 38:3). They journeyed with the altar (Num 4:14), and Hiram cast them again for Solomon’s temple: “Hiram made the lavers, and the shovels, and the basons” (1Ki 7:40). Of all the vessels the shovel does the lowliest work, for it handles the ash—the spent remains of what has been wholly burned to God. Yet Scripture counts this office holy, for the ashes of the offering are precious: they are the token that the sacrifice was accepted and consumed, and the priest bore them forth to a clean place (Lev 6:10-11). The shovel therefore honours what men despise, the leavings of a finished sacrifice. It preaches that in the house of God there is no mean labour: the same brass that fronts the altar also carries out its ashes, and both are the LORD’s. Here is a rebuke to every pride that would serve God only in the conspicuous office. The hand that clears the ashes, if it clears them for Him, does a sacred work; for even the cinders of the altar are holy unto the LORD.
webster_summary: The brazen altar-scoops, made to lift away the ashes of the sacrifices—the lowliest office counted holy.
webster_full: SHOVELS, instruments with a broad blade for lifting and casting loose matter, as ashes.
Numbered among the brazen vessels of the altar (Exo 27:3; Exo 38:3).
Their office was to remove the ashes of the burnt offerings.
Recast in brass by Hiram for Solomon’s temple (1Ki 7:40).
A figure that no labour about the altar of God is mean or common.

corruption_summary: A humble vessel of the altar, not a contested doctrine; the shovel recovers the honour of lowly service and the sacredness of the small.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the shovel rebukes is the age’s contempt for small and hidden things—the craving to serve, if at all, only in the seen and celebrated office, and to despise the labour that leaves no name. But the God who ordained the shovel counts the clearing of ashes among the vessels of His altar. The world weighs work by its show; the sanctuary weighs it by the LORD it is done unto, and there the ash-scoop is brass as holy as the altar it serves.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of humble service: the ashes of the offering are precious, the token of a sacrifice accepted, and the hand that clears them for God does a sacred work. Whatsoever is done, done heartily as to the Lord (Col 3:23), is great in His house, though the world see only cinders.

etymology: From Old French bacin, a wide vessel; the older English spelling of basins, rendering Hebrew mizrāq—the bowls of the altar that caught and cast the sacrificial blood.
biblical_def: Basons are the wide bowls of the sanctuary, and chief among their uses was the handling of blood: they caught the blood of the sacrifices and bore it to be sprinkled upon and about the altar. They are numbered among the brazen vessels, “his shovels, and his basons, and his fleshhooks” (Exo 27:3), and in the temple they were of gold (1Ch 28:17). At the sealing of the covenant at Sinai, “Moses took half of the blood, and put it in basons; and half of the blood he sprinkled on the altar” (Exo 24:6)—the very vessels that bound Israel to the LORD in blood. So the bason is the vessel of the blood, and the blood is the life, and the life poured out makes atonement (Lev 17:11). Every day the priests filled these bowls at the altar and cast the crimson against its sides, a ceaseless witness that without shedding of blood is no remission (Heb 9:22). All this pointed forward: the basons of brass and gold could only carry the blood of beasts, which cannot take away sin; but they preached the Blood that could. When Zechariah foretells the LORD’s people made mighty, they are “filled like bowls, and as the corners of the altar” (Zec 9:15)—filled as the blood-bowls of the sanctuary, dedicated wholly to God. The bason teaches that at the centre of true worship stands atoning blood.
webster_summary: The wide altar-bowls that caught and cast the sacrificial blood—vessels that preach atonement at the heart of worship.
webster_full: BASONS, wide, hollow vessels or bowls (the older spelling of basins).

The vessels of the covenant-blood sprinkled at Sinai (Exo 24:6).
A figure of worship centred on atoning blood (Heb 9:22).

corruption_summary: A bowl of the altar, not a contested doctrine; the bason recovers the blood at the centre of worship, which the age would gladly forget.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the bason rebukes is the modern flight from blood—the wish for a worship swept clean of sacrifice, a gospel without an altar, a religion of sentiment that finds the crimson bowls of Scripture crude. But the God of the sanctuary set the blood-bason at the heart of His house and never took it thence, for without shedding of blood is no remission. To empty worship of atonement is to keep the temple and lose the reason for it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the centrality of atoning blood: the basons caught the life poured out (Lev 17:11), and all their sprinkling pointed to the Blood of Christ, which alone cleanseth from all sin (1Jn 1:7). True worship does not blush at the bason; it glories in the Lamb slain, and is filled like the bowls of the altar, wholly the LORD’s.

etymology: From Old French chargeour, a vessel that is loaded or charged; rendering Hebrew q'ārāh and Greek pinax—a large deep dish or platter for bearing an offering.
biblical_def: A charger is a great dish or platter, a vessel loaded (or “charged”) with an offering to be borne before the LORD. In the dedication of the tabernacle altar each prince of Israel brought “one silver charger… full of fine flour mingled with oil for a meat offering” (Num 7:13), and the sum was reckoned, “twelve chargers of silver” (Num 7:84), a laden dish for every tribe. Among the vessels Cyrus restored from Babylon were “thirty chargers of gold, a thousand chargers of silver” (Ezr 1:9)—the holy platters carried into exile and brought home again. So in its proper place the charger is a vessel of glad and costly worship, heaped with the best and offered to God. But the word bears one dark occurrence that Scripture will not let us forget: at Herod’s feast the daughter of Herodias asked, “Give me here John Baptist’s head in a charger” (Mat 14:8). The platter that was made to bear an offering to God was made to bear the head of God’s prophet to a wanton woman. Here two altars stand opposed—the LORD’s, laden with fine flour and oil, and the world’s, laden with the blood of a righteous man to please a dancer. The charger asks every soul what it will heap upon its dish: an offering to God, or a trophy of sin.
webster_summary: A great platter for bearing an offering—laden with fine flour before the LORD, or with a prophet’s head at Herod’s feast.
webster_full: CHARGERS, large dishes or platters, so called as being charged or loaded.

Chargers of gold and silver restored from Babylon by Cyrus (Ezr 1:9).
The platter that bore John the Baptist’s head at Herod’s feast (Mat 14:8).
A vessel that displays what a man will heap upon it, offering or trophy.

corruption_summary: A platter of offering, not a contested doctrine; the charger recovers the solemn question of what a man loads upon his dish, offering or trophy of sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the charger sets before us is written in its two great uses. The princes charged their platters with fine flour and oil and set them before the LORD; Herodias charged hers with the head of a prophet to gratify a grudge. The age still heaps its chargers—with pleasures, prizes, and the ruin of the righteous who reprove it—and calls the feast a celebration. Every laden dish is an offering to someone; the question is only to whom.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that worship is costly and deliberate: the tribes brought their best, heaped and weighed, to the altar of God. Let a man charge his life-dish with fine flour, an offering acceptable and well-pleasing (Rom 12:1), and not with the trophies of sin; for what we lay upon the charger declares what we love.

etymology: From Old English spōn, a chip or shaving of wood, hence a hollowed vessel; rendering Hebrew kaph, a palm or hollow of the hand—the golden incense-cups of the sanctuary.
biblical_def: The spoons of the sanctuary are not the spoons of the table but golden incense-cups, hollowed dishes (Hebrew kaph, a “palm”) that held the frankincense set beside the shewbread and offered at the altar. They belong to the furniture of the golden table: “the dishes thereof, and spoons thereof, and covers thereof, and bowls thereof… of pure gold shalt thou make them” (Exo 25:29), and upon the table of shewbread the priests laid “the dishes, and the spoons, and the bowls” with the continual bread (Num 4:7). At the altar’s dedication each prince brought “one spoon of ten shekels of gold, full of incense” (Num 7:14)—the little cup laden with perfume. Incense throughout Scripture is the figure of prayer, that ascends as a sweet savour before God (Psa 141:2; Rev 5:8); and the spoon is the small golden vessel that bears it. Herein is a gentle lesson: the vessel of prayer need not be great, but it must be pure gold and full. Ten shekels of gold, but full of incense—so the prayers of the saints, small in the world’s eyes, are precious and pleasing when they are pure and full of Christ. When Babylon plundered the temple “the spoons… took they away” (2Ki 25:14); yet the true incense of prayer no captivity can silence, for it rises still before the throne.
webster_summary: The golden incense-cups of the sanctuary—small vessels, pure and full, bearing the sweet perfume that figures prayer.

corruption_summary: A golden incense-cup, not a contested doctrine; the spoon recovers the worth of small, pure, and full vessels of prayer.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the spoon rebukes is the age’s scorn of the small—the notion that only the great, the loud, and the many are worth God’s regard, and that a little offered in secret is nothing. But the LORD counted every golden spoon of ten shekels, and every one full of incense. Heaven does not weigh prayer as the world weighs it; the widow’s mite and the hidden petition are golden vessels before Him, if they be pure and full.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the vessel of prayer must be pure gold and full: not great, but genuine; not showy, but filled with the sweet incense of a heart set on Christ. The prayers of the saints are golden vials before the throne (Rev 5:8), and no captivity can carry away the incense that ascends from a faithful heart.

etymology: From Old French flacon, a large flask; rendering Hebrew words for a vessel of wine (and, in some places, a pressed cake of raisins)—the drink-vessels associated with the sanctuary and with feasting.
biblical_def: Flagons are large vessels for wine, and in Scripture they gather up the drink offering and the fulness of the sanctuary’s table. Among the pure-gold furniture of the golden table were the “covers thereof, and bowls thereof, to cover withal” (Exo 25:29), the vessels from which the drink offering was poured out before the LORD. The flagon speaks of provision and of gladness in God’s house: when David had set the ark in its place, “he dealt to every one of Israel… a good piece of flesh, and a flagon of wine” (1Ch 16:3), that the people should rejoice before the LORD. In the Song, the sick-of-love bride cries, “Stay me with flagons, comfort me with apples: for I am sick of love” (Son 2:5)—the flagon a figure of the strong comfort the soul seeks in her Beloved. Yet Isaiah sounds a warning: all the glory hung upon Eliakim, “all vessels of small quantity, from the vessels of cups, even to all the vessels of flagons” (Isa 22:24), shall in the day of overloading break and fall. So the flagon holds two truths together: that God fills His people with wine of gladness and strong consolation, and that no earthly vessel, however laden with glory, can bear the weight men hang upon it. The wine of true and lasting joy is His alone to give.
webster_summary: Large wine-vessels of provision and gladness—the strong comfort of God’s house, and a warning against the vessel overladen.

corruption_summary: A vessel of wine and gladness, not a contested doctrine; the flagon recovers the true source of comfort and warns against the vessel overladen.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the flagon rebukes is the age’s search for strong comfort in every flagon but the LORD’s—drinking of pleasure, drink, and diversion to stay a soul that is sick, and finding the wine turn to gall. Scripture does not forbid gladness; God Himself dealt out the flagon that His people might rejoice. But it warns that the vessels of earth, laden with all our glory and all our hope, will crack and fall in the day of trial (Isa 22:24).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the true source of comfort: it is Christ who stays the love-sick soul, whose love is better than wine (Son 1:2), and whose Spirit fills the heart with a gladness no flagon of the world can pour. Be not drunk with wine, but filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18); the lasting flagon is the LORD’s alone.

etymology: A compound of snuff (the charred wick) and dish; rendering Hebrew machtāh—the small golden trays of the candlestick that received the cropped and smoking wick.
biblical_def: Snuffdishes are the little golden trays of the candlestick, made to receive the burnt wick that the snuffers cropped away. They come always in the company of the light: “The tongs thereof, and the snuffdishes thereof, shall be of pure gold” (Exo 25:38), and Bezaleel wrought them so, “his seven lamps, and his snuffers, and his snuffdishes, of pure gold” (Exo 37:23). When the camp journeyed, the Kohathites covered the candlestick “and his tongs, and his snuffdishes, and all the oil vessels thereof” under a cloth of blue (Num 4:9). So slight a vessel, named but three times, yet it too was of pure gold and had its holy office: to carry away the dead and smoking wick, that nothing charred should defile the light which was to give light before the candlestick continually (Num 8:2). Here is a lowly and precious lesson. The lamp of testimony must not only be trimmed by the snuffers; the trimmings must be gathered up and borne away, lest the very refuse of the flame lie smoking in the holy place. God appoints a golden vessel even for the wick’s ash. So in the life of His people the dead thing, once cropped, must be carried clean away—confessed, removed, not left to smoulder—that the light burn pure. Even the disposal of the sanctuary’s refuse was gold, for all about the light of God is holy.
webster_summary: The little golden trays of the candlestick that received the cropped and smoking wick—even the flame’s refuse borne away in gold.

corruption_summary: A little vessel of the candlestick, not a contested doctrine; the snuffdish recovers the truth that the flame’s dead refuse must be borne clean away.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the snuffdish rebukes is the leaving of dead things to smoulder in the holy place—the sin cropped in word but never carried away, the charred wick of an old fault left lying near the light to smoke and stain. The age is content to trim what it will not remove, to confess without forsaking; but the sanctuary gave a golden dish to bear the wick’s ash quite away, that no dead thing lie smoking where God’s light must burn.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is thoroughness in mortification: it is not enough that the dead be cropped by the snuffers; it must be gathered and borne clean out, confessed and forsaken (Pro 28:13). God counts even the flame’s refuse worth a vessel of pure gold; let His people not leave smouldering what His grace has cut away.
